items: Open **Equilibrium Lab → Aqueous Reaction → Equilibrium** (the link ends in ?subUnitId=eqm.aqueous.equilibrium).
Read each box and click **Next**. On the **Choose a reaction!** screen, open the menu and look at all three reactions.

items.prompt: You put only A and B into water. Which reaction can happen first, the forward or the reverse? Why?
items.answer: Forward. There are no products (C, D) yet, so the reverse reaction has nothing to start from. Accept: forward, because only reactants are present.

items: Some reactions don't go to completion, but as they are {{reversible}}, they move towards {{equilibrium}}.
Reversible means there's a {{forward}} reaction that makes the products, and a {{reverse}} reaction that makes reactants.
**Chemical equilibrium** means both forward and reverse reactions have the {{same rate}}.

blocks.title: Data table
blocks.subtitle: Write Q for each reaction in the menu (products on top, coefficients become powers)

items.prompt: The sim uses **K = 10** for every aqueous reaction (you will see it on the next page). The sim does not show the next two, so use K = 10. (a) What is K for the reverse reaction C + D ⇌ A + B? (b) What is K for 2A + 2B ⇌ 2C + 2D?
items.answer: (a) K(reverse) = 1/K = 1/10 = **0.10**. (b) Doubling every coefficient squares K: 10² = **100**.

items.prompt: A classmate says, "At equilibrium the reaction has stopped." Use the sim's definition to correct this.
items.answer: The reaction has not stopped: the forward and reverse reactions keep going at the same rate, so the amounts stay constant. Accept: dynamic equilibrium, equal rates, constant concentrations.

items: Open **Reaction Quotient** (?subUnitId=eqm.aqueous.quotient). It always uses **A + B ⇌ C + D**. Set the water to any level (it doesn't change the numbers).

At **Shake them into the beaker**, shake **A** until [A] in the Q equation (top right) reads **0.30** and stops rising (about 15 shakes). Do the same for **B**. Click **Next**. Do the **Calculate** box before you open the **Table** tab above the graph.

items.prompt: Right after you add A and B (no C or D yet), what is Q? Is Q bigger or smaller than K?
items.answer: Q = 0, because the top of the fraction ([C][D]) is 0. Q < K, so the forward reaction runs.

items: **Q, the reaction quotient**, is the {{product}} concentration divided by the {{reactant}} concentration, each raised to its {{stoichiometric coefficient}}.
If the reaction is in equilibrium, the value of {{Q}} and {{K}} will be the same.
The larger the products, the {{larger}} Q. When using concentrations, K is often called {{Kc}}.
The forward reaction is {{favored}}, because products must be produced to reach equilibrium.

items.prompt: Use an ICE table with K = 10. Start: [A] = [B] = 0.30 M, [C] = [D] = 0. Find the equilibrium concentrations. (Hint: x²/(0.30 − x)² = 10, so take the square root of both sides.)

blocks.subtitle: After the reaction finishes, click the Table tab and copy the ICE table

blocks.prompt: Sketch the Q graph (Q vs. time). Draw and label the K line.
blocks.answer: Q starts at 0, rises quickly, then slows and levels off exactly on the K line (Q = K = 10).

items.prompt: **Free Explore**: start with A = B = 0.10, C = D = 0.20, then with A = B = 0.05, C = D = 0.25. Find each starting Q and the direction. Why do both end at [A] = 0.072, [C] = 0.23?
items.answer: Start 1: Q = 0.20²/0.10² = 4 < 10 → forward. Start 2: Q = 0.25²/0.05² = 25 > 10 → reverse. Both mixes hold the same total A + C (0.30) and B + D (0.30), so they reach the same equilibrium from opposite sides.

items: Open **Le Chatelier's Principle** (?subUnitId=eqm.aqueous.lechatelier). It starts from its own equilibrium of A + B ⇌ C + D (it began with [A] = 0.30 and [B] = 0.26).
Read the Q equation: [A] = 0.088, [B] = 0.051, [C] = 0.21. Copy the Table tab's **Final** row into the first row of the data table.
At **Shake C and D into the beaker**, shake **C** until [C] reads **0.30** and stops (about 5 shakes). Do the same for **D**.

items.prompt: You add more product (C and D). Which reaction will be favored? What will happen to [A]?
items.answer: The reverse reaction; [A] (and [B]) will go up while [C] and [D] go down a little.

items: Le Chatelier observed that any variation done to a system in equilibrium would make the system {{counteract}}.
After adding C and D, the {{reverse}} reaction is favored, because {{reactants}} must be produced to reach equilibrium.
At equilibrium the concentrations are not {{equal}}, just {{constant}}.

items.prompt: Right after you add C and D: [A] = 0.088, [B] = 0.051, [C] = [D] = 0.30. Calculate Q and compare it with K = 10 before the reaction runs.
Use the new equilibrium values to show that K did not change.
items.answer: Q = 0.28² / (0.11 × 0.07) = 10.2 ≈ 10 = K (rounding). Adding C and D changed Q, not K.

items.prompt: [C] was 0.21, jumped to 0.30, and ended at 0.28. Did the system undo the whole change? Explain with Le Chatelier's principle.
items.answer: No. It used up only about 0.02 M of the added C, so [C] ends higher than before (0.28 > 0.21). The system partly counteracts the change until Q = K again.

blocks.text: **Le Chatelier Free Explore** (eqm.aqueous.lechatelier.free-explore): set **Add A** to 0.10 and the others to 0. Predict the direction before you click start, then check the graph.

items: Open **Gaseous Reaction → Partial Pressure** (?subUnitId=eqm.gaseous.partial-pressure). At **Choose a reaction!** pick **3A + 4B ⇌ C + 2D** (the first one).
At **Use the pump**: pump **A** until P_A in the Q equation reads **1.5** and stops (about 35 pumps). Flip the switch under the pump to **B** and pump B to **1.5** too. Click **Next**.
The sim shows no units; we use atm for partial pressures.

items.prompt: Which partial pressure will drop more as the reaction runs, P_A or P_B? Why?
items.answer: P_B: the reaction uses 4 B for every 3 A, so B drops faster.

items: In the gaseous reaction, {{partial pressures}} of compounds are used instead of the concentrations.
In this case we talk about {{Kp}} (p stands for {{pressure}}).
The forward reaction runs until Q = {{Kp}}, as the products to reactants ratio is still {{lower}} than at equilibrium.
Q = {{P_C · P_D² / (P_A³ · P_B⁴)}}        Kp = {{10}}

items.prompt: At equilibrium P_C has gone up by x = 0.274 atm. Use the coefficients to find the change in P_A, P_B and P_D, and all four final pressures, before you open the Table tab.
Plug your final pressures into Q. Is Q = Kp?

blocks.subtitle: Click the Table tab and copy the ICE table (partial pressures)

items.prompt: At the start, the scale under the Q panel tips toward the reactant side. What does that tell you about Q compared with Kp, and which way the reaction must go?
items.answer: Q < Kp (Q = 0 at the start), so the reactant side is "heavier" and the forward reaction is favored until Q = Kp and the scale is level.

blocks.text: **Partial Pressure Free Explore**: pick A + 2B ⇌ 4C + 3D, set A = B = 1.0 and C = D = 0, and watch which way it goes. Then add some C and D before you start and predict again.

items: Open **Pressure Changes** (?subUnitId=eqm.gaseous.pressure). It starts from a saved equilibrium of 3A + 4B ⇌ C + 2D, Kp = 10 (not your numbers from the last page).
The Table tab's Final row shows the start: P_A = 0.74, P_B = 0.36, P_C = 0.25, P_D = 0.51 atm.
At **Use the slider**, drag the slider next to the beaker (the piston) **all the way down** (smallest volume). Then click **Next**.

items.prompt: Which side of 3A + 4B ⇌ C + 2D has fewer moles of gas? When you squeeze the gas, which way will it shift?
items.answer: Products: 1 + 2 = 3 mol vs. reactants 3 + 4 = 7 mol. It shifts forward (right), toward fewer moles of gas.

items: Decreased container volume {{increases}} pressure, increasing the species concentration.
Since {{reactants}} have higher exponents, Q {{decreases}}.
The {{forward}} reaction {{consumes}} gas. As you increased the pressure, the system will favor this reaction to reach equilibrium.

items.prompt: All the way down, the volume is 0.48 of the starting volume, so every partial pressure is multiplied by 1/0.48 = 2.08. (a) Find the four new pressures. (b) Find Q and compare it with Kp. (Shortcut: Q = Kp × 2.08^(1 + 2 − 3 − 4).)

blocks.subtitle: After the shift, copy the Table tab (Initial = right after you moved the piston)

items.prompt: What was Kp before and after you moved the piston? Explain why squeezing the gas shifts the reaction even though Kp stays the same.
items.answer: Kp = 10 both times (Q = Kp panel). Squeezing multiplies every pressure by 2.08, but the reactant side has bigger powers (7 vs. 3), so Q drops to 0.53. The forward reaction (fewer gas moles) runs until Q is back to 10. Only Q changed, not Kp.

blocks.text: **Pressure Changes Free Explore**: drag the piston **all the way up** (bigger volume, lower pressure). Predict the direction before you start the run. Which side makes more moles of gas?

items: Open **Temperature Changes** (?subUnitId=eqm.gaseous.temperature). It starts at a saved equilibrium (P_A = 1.09, P_B = 0.42, P_C = 0.46, P_D = 0.93 atm, Kp = 10). The reaction shows **+ Heat** on the products side.
At **use the flame slider**, drag the slider under the beaker **all the way to the right**. Read the new Kp in the Q = Kp panel.

items.prompt: Heat is written as a product. If you add heat, which way should the reaction shift? Should Kp go up or down?
items.answer: To the left (reverse), to use up the added heat. Kp goes down.

items: Raising the temperature makes the system try to {{consume}} heat, so the reaction favored will be the {{endothermic}} one.
In this reaction, the forward reaction is {{exothermic}}, while the reverse is {{endothermic}}.
With the flame all the way up, Kp changes from 10 to {{1.0}}.

items.prompt: Right after heating, the pressures have not changed yet. What is Q? Compare it with the new Kp and give the direction.
items.answer: Q is still **10** (it was at equilibrium). New Kp = 1.0, so Q > Kp: the **reverse** reaction is favored.

blocks.subtitle: After the shift, copy the Table tab

items.prompt: Show that the final pressures fit the new Kp.
Compare this page with Pressure Changes. Which change altered the value of Kp, and which only altered Q? Use the sim's numbers.
items.answer: Heating changed Kp itself (10 → 1.0), so the old pressures (Q = 10) were no longer at equilibrium. Squeezing the gas left Kp at 10 and changed only Q (10 → 0.53).

blocks.text: **Temperature Changes Free Explore**: put the flame slider near the middle and start the run. Is the new Kp between 1.0 and 10? Is the shift bigger or smaller than with the full flame?

items: Open **Solubility → Ionic Compounds** (?subUnitId=eqm.solubility.ionic). At **Choose a reaction!** pick **AB(s) ⇌ A⁺ + B⁻** (the first one). Click **Next** through every screen, watching the Q panel and the recap screen.
Some reactions can produce solids as their products; these are called {{precipitation reactions}}. As they are reversible, the solid can also {{dissolve}}.
The measurement of how much a salt can dissolve in water is called {{solubility}}.
A salt is dissolved when it turns into {{ions}}. In this type of reaction we work with the {{net-ionic}} equation.
AB(s) is not included in Q, because pure {{solids}} and {{liquids}} are not included.

blocks.subtitle: The recap screen and the Q panel: write Q for each kind of reaction

items.prompt: The sim only has 1:1 salts. Write the Ksp expression for a real salt, CaF₂(s) ⇌ Ca²⁺(aq) + 2F⁻(aq) (not in the sim).
items.answer: Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]² (no CaF₂ term; the coefficient 2 becomes a power).

items: Open **Solubility Product** (?subUnitId=eqm.solubility.product). The salt is AB(s); this sim uses **Ksp = 0.10** (a made-up salt that dissolves far more than real ones).
Set the water with the slider (any level; it does not change the numbers).
Shake **AB(s)** in (each shake adds 125 mg) until the sim says equilibrium (15 shakes). When asked, shake in more AB(s) until it stops. Do the **Calculate** box before you open the **Table** tab.

items.prompt: What will happen to extra AB(s) you add after Q reaches Ksp?
items.answer: It stays solid on the bottom; it does not dissolve and Q stays equal to Ksp.

items: That's why K is called {{Ksp}}; Ksp stands for {{solubility product}}.
The higher the Ksp, the {{higher}} the amount of ions the reaction produces at equilibrium.
Once Q reaches Ksp, the forward and reverse reactions go at the {{same rate}}, so no more solid can be turned into ions.
You could only dissolve {{1875}} mg of AB(s).
Extra solid doesn't affect Q, as it is still Q = Ksp. The solution has reached its {{capacity}} to dissolve the salt: it is {{saturated}}.

items.prompt: Ksp = [A⁺][B⁻] = 0.10, and each AB that dissolves makes one A⁺ and one B⁻. Let s = molar solubility. Find s.

blocks.subtitle: Click the Table tab and copy it

blocks.prompt: Sketch the Q graph (Q vs. time), including the time when you added extra solid. Label the K line.
blocks.answer: Q rises from 0 and levels off on the K line (0.10). It stays flat on the K line when extra solid is added.

items.prompt: The sim says Ksp is like "the maximum amount of ions that can be in a solution." Make this more exact using your numbers.
items.answer: Ksp is the largest value of the product [A⁺][B⁻] (0.10) a saturated solution can hold. Each ion is 0.32 M, not 0.10 M. Accept: Ksp is a product of ion concentrations, not an amount.

blocks.text: **Solubility Product Free Explore**: set Solid added to 1000 mg and start. Is Q less than, equal to, or greater than Ksp? Is the solution saturated? Then try 2500 mg.

items: Open **Common Ion Effect** (?subUnitId=eqm.solubility.common-ion); Ksp is still 0.10. Shake **XB(s)** in until it stops (4 shakes = 500 mg): [B⁻] becomes **0.12** M.
Then shake **AB(s)** in until the sim says equilibrium (11 shakes), and add extra when asked. Do the **Calculate** box before you open the **Table** tab.

items.prompt: With B⁻ already in the water, will more or less AB(s) dissolve than on the last page? Why?
items.answer: Less. B⁻ is a product of AB(s) ⇌ A⁺ + B⁻, so Q is already partly "filled" and the reaction reaches Ksp sooner.

items: When an ion is already in the solution, the salt won't be as {{soluble}}. This is called the {{common-ion effect}}.
The common ion in this situation is {{B⁻}}. X⁺ {{doesn't}} affect the solubility of AB(s).
You could only dissolve {{1375}} mg of AB(s), which is {{less}} than before.

items.prompt: Ksp = 0.10 and [B⁻] starts at 0.12 M. Let s = molar solubility of AB. Solve s(0.12 + s) = 0.10 with the quadratic formula. Find [A⁺] and [B⁻].

blocks.subtitle: Click the Table tab and copy it

items.prompt: Compare the molar solubility of AB with and without the common ion (Solubility Product page). By what percent did it drop? Explain with Le Chatelier's principle.
items.answer: 0.32 M → 0.26 M, about **17%** lower. Adding B⁻ (a product) shifts AB(s) ⇌ A⁺ + B⁻ to the left, so less solid dissolves before Q = Ksp.

blocks.text: **Common Ion Free Explore**: set Common ion added to 250 mg (half as much B⁻) and Solid added to 1375 mg. Predict: will [A⁺] end between 0.26 and 0.32? Check the Q panel.

items: Open **pH Effect** (?subUnitId=eqm.solubility.ph). It starts where the Common Ion page ended: saturated, [A⁺] = 0.26 M, [B⁻] = 0.38 M, extra AB(s) on the bottom.
At **Shake H+ ions into the beaker!**, shake **H⁺** in one shake at a time. Record Q after each of the first 5 shakes. The 6th shake starts the dissolving right away.

items.prompt: H⁺ reacts with B⁻. What do you think will happen to the extra solid on the bottom?
items.answer: It dissolves: removing B⁻ lowers Q below Ksp, so the forward (dissolving) reaction runs.

items: Lower pH values mean higher presence of {{H⁺}} ions. In this case, H⁺ reacts with B⁻ to form {{HB(aq)}}.
Adding H⁺ reduces the B⁻ ions in the solution, {{reducing Q}}, allowing AB(s) to turn into more ions.
The solution is no longer {{saturated}}, and the {{forward}} reaction is favored until equilibrium.

blocks.subtitle: Q from the Q panel after each H⁺ shake

items.prompt: [A⁺] stays at 0.26 M while you add H⁺, and Q drops about 0.012 per shake. (a) How much [B⁻] does each shake remove? (b) Predict [B⁻] and Q right after the 6th shake.
Find the new equilibrium: (0.26 + x)(0.11 + x) = 0.10. Then check your answer with the Q panel at the end.

blocks.prompt: Sketch the Solubility vs. pH curve below the Q panel and show where the red dot moves (shape only; the curve is not to scale).
blocks.answer: A U-shaped curve, lowest in the middle. The red dot sits on the high-pH arm, then moves left toward low pH as H⁺ is added.

items.prompt: Claim: lowering the pH made AB more soluble. Give evidence with numbers from this page.
items.answer: [A⁺], which equals the AB dissolved, rose from 0.26 M to 0.40 M and the extra solid dissolved. Accept: Q fell below Ksp (0.029 < 0.10), so more solid dissolved.

blocks.text: **pH Effect Free Explore**: set Solid present to 1000 mg and Acid added to 6. Does all the solid dissolve? Is Q equal to Ksp at the end, or less? What does that say about saturation?

conclusion.prompt: In every part of this lab, one comparison told you which way the reaction would go. Name it, and give one example with numbers from each part (aqueous, gaseous, solubility).
conclusion.answer: Compare Q with K. Aqueous: Q = 20 > K = 10 after adding C and D → reverse. Gaseous: Q = 0.53 < Kp = 10 after squeezing → forward. Solubility: Q = 0.029 < Ksp = 0.10 after adding H⁺ → dissolves. Accept any correct example per part.

conclusion.prompt: List the changes you made in this lab. Which one changed the value of K, and which only changed Q?
conclusion.answer: Only heating changed K (Kp 10 → 1.0). Adding C and D, changing the volume, adding the common ion B⁻ and adding H⁺ changed only Q; K stayed the same.

conclusion.prompt: Both the common ion and H⁺ change [B⁻]. Explain why one lowers the solubility of AB and the other raises it.
conclusion.answer: The common ion adds B⁻, so Q is larger and the equilibrium shifts left: s drops from 0.32 to 0.26 M. H⁺ removes B⁻ (as HB), so Q drops below Ksp and the equilibrium shifts right: s rises from 0.26 to 0.40 M.

key_notes: All reactions are hypothetical (A, B, C, D; AB, XB). K = 10 for every aqueous reaction (features/lessons/aqueous/lesson.tsx:16), Kp = 10 at the start of every gaseous module (gaseous/lesson.tsx:22), Ksp = 0.1 (solubility/lesson.tsx:55). A real sparingly soluble salt has a far smaller Ksp; the worksheet calls this a made-up salt.
The sim shows no units. The worksheet uses M for concentrations and atm for partial pressures.

Each module loads its own saved starting state, even when students click Next from the module before. So the reaction picked in the Equilibrium module is reset to A + B ⇌ C + D in Reaction Quotient; Le Chatelier starts from [A] = 0.30, [B] = 0.263; Pressure Changes and Temperature Changes start from saved equilibria; pH Effect starts after the common-ion step (data/presets/index.ts:36–153, 291–298; useAqueousLessonController.tsx:201–218).

The Q panel rounds to 2 significant figures and then adjusts the second product term so the shown Q matches. Students can see [D] = 0.214 next to [C] = 0.21, P_D = 0.522, or [A⁺] = 0.32 next to [B⁻] = 0.313 in pure water (displayNumbers.ts:38–93). The worksheet has students copy the Table tab (2 decimals) instead, and only reads the panel where the value is not adjusted.
The Table tab shows the equilibrium answer as soon as the reactants are in. Have students finish the Calculate box first.
Shaking adds 0.02 M per shake up to 0.30 M (aqueous); the pump adds 0.043 atm per pump up to 1.5 atm; each solid shake adds 125 mg. "Shake until it stops" makes every student's numbers match.

Piston slider: all the way down gives 0.48 × the starting volume (pressures × 2.08); all the way up gives 1.52 × (worked out from AirBeaker.tsx:219–224, GaseousBeaker.tsx:126, 158 and the fixed width 280 in routes/…/gaseous.tsx:96). The sim never shows the volume.

Flame slider: Kp = 10 × 10^(−slider), slider 0–1 (useGaseousLessonController.tsx:531). The handle starts in the middle, but the sim counts the start as 0, so full right gives Kp = 1.0. Any position past 0.40 counts as a raise, even if a student dragged the handle left of where it started.
Water-level sliders (aqueous and solubility) are only visual; no number depends on them. In real life, more water dissolves more grams of salt.
The sim's 1875 mg and 1375 mg are not in the same ratio as the molar solubilities (73% vs. 83%), so the worksheet uses molar solubility (0.32 → 0.26 M) for the percent drop.

pH Effect: each H⁺ shake removes a fixed 0.045 M of B⁻ (made-up constant, solubility/lesson.tsx:63). No pH value is ever shown, and the Solubility vs. pH curve is a hand-drawn U shape, so ask only for shape.
Checking Q with 2-decimal table values gives 9.5–10.8 instead of exactly 10. Accept "≈ 10".

ap_topics: 7.5 Magnitude of the Equilibrium Constant (partly: K is 10, 1.0 and 0.10 only)
7.10 Reaction Quotient and Le Châtelier's Principle
lesson_plan.sim_location: ChemSims.app → Simulations → Equilibrium Lab (Aqueous, Gaseous and Solubility modules)
lesson_plan.essential_question: How does a reversible reaction "know" which way to go, and how does it respond when we disturb it?
objectives: Write Q and K (Kc, Kp, Ksp) expressions, leaving out pure solids.
Compare Q with K to predict the direction of a reaction.
Use ICE tables to find equilibrium concentrations and partial pressures.
Explain shifts from concentration, volume and temperature changes with Le Châtelier's principle and Q.
Calculate molar solubility from Ksp, with and without a common ion, and explain the effect of pH.
prep: Open each module from its ?subUnitId= link once. Note that every module starts from its own saved state (see Sim cautions).
Decide whether students may use the Table tab before the Calculate box; we recommend "calculate first, then check."

The sim doesn't cover 7.6 Properties of the Equilibrium Constant (beyond the short calc on p. 1), 7.14 Free Energy of Dissolution, Kc–Kp conversion, or salts that aren't 1:1. Use your usual lesson for these.

days.title: Teacher demo: what equilibrium means
days.goal: Students see that reversible reactions move toward a balance of equal rates, and write Q for the sim's three reactions.
agenda: Warm-up: "Can a reaction run backward?" (pairs, 1 sentence)
Demo of the Equilibrium module (script below); students fill in p. 1
Whole class: Q expressions in the p. 1 table; K for the reverse reaction
Hand out worksheets; preview the Reaction Quotient module

demo_script.do: Project ChemSims.app → Equilibrium Lab → Aqueous Reaction → Equilibrium (?subUnitId=eqm.aqueous.equilibrium). Read the first box aloud.
demo_script.say: "Some reactions don't go to completion." What do you think happens instead?
demo_script.students: Guided notes 1–2: reversible, equilibrium, forward, reverse.

demo_script.do: Before clicking Next, ask the Predict question.
demo_script.say: If I only put A and B in water, which reaction can start? (Expected: forward, since no products exist yet.)

demo_script.do: Click Next. Open the **Choose a reaction!** menu and show all three reactions.
demo_script.say: These reactions are made up, but the coefficients matter. Which reaction has more reactant moles than product moles? (Expected: 3A + 2B ⇌ C + 2D.)
demo_script.students: Column 1 and the coefficient sums in the data table.

demo_script.do: Write Q for A + B ⇌ C + D on the board: products over reactants.
demo_script.say: Products on top, reactants on the bottom, coefficients become powers. Try the other two with a partner.
demo_script.students: Q expressions for rows 2 and 3 of the table.

demo_script.say: Why does D get a 4th power in the last one? (Expected: its coefficient is 4.)

demo_script.do: Click Next to the **Chemical equilibrium** box. Read it aloud.
demo_script.say: At equilibrium, are the reactions still running? (Expected: yes, at the same rate.)

demo_script.do: Tell students the sim uses K = 10 for these reactions. Work the reverse-reaction K together.
demo_script.say: If K forward = 10, what is K for C + D ⇌ A + B? (Expected: 1/10 = 0.10.) What if we double every coefficient? (Expected: 10² = 100.)

demo_script.do: Pose the Analyze question; take 2–3 answers.
demo_script.say: "At equilibrium the reaction has stopped." True or false? Use the sim's words.
demo_script.students: Analyze box, p. 1: dynamic, equal rates.

days.title: Student sim work: aqueous Q, ICE and Le Châtelier
days.goal: Use Q vs. K to predict direction and solve an ICE table; see a concentration disturbance.
agenda: Review Q vs. K: Q < K forward, Q > K reverse
p. 2 Reaction Quotient (calculate before opening Table)
circulate: Both A and B shaken all the way to 0.30 (the Q panel shows (0.30)).
The ICE calc is done before the Table tab is opened.
In Le Chatelier, C and D shaken until 0.30; Q after adding = 20.
Students copy the Table tab, not the Q panel (the panel can show 0.214 for D).
days.checkpoint: Reaction Quotient equilibrium: [A] = [B] = 0.072 M, [C] = [D] = 0.23 M; Le Chatelier Q after adding C and D = 20 > K.
days.early_finishers: Both Free Explore runs on p. 2; then Le Chatelier Free Explore with Add A = 0.10.

days.title: Student sim work: gaseous Kp, pressure and temperature
days.goal: Use Kp and partial pressures; contrast a volume change (changes Q) with a temperature change (changes K).
days.worksheet_pages: pp. 4–6 (Partial Pressure, Pressure Changes, Temperature Changes)
agenda: Warm-up: count gas moles on each side of 3A + 4B ⇌ C + 2D
circulate: Reaction 3A + 4B ⇌ C + 2D picked; both A and B pumped to 1.5 (switch flipped to B).
Piston dragged all the way DOWN on p. 5 (Initial row 1.53, 0.75, 0.53, 1.06).
Flame slider all the way RIGHT on p. 6; Kp panel reads 1.0.
Students ignore the sim's line "the forward reaction is being favored" after heating; the reverse is favored.
days.checkpoint: After squeezing: Q = 0.53 < Kp = 10 (forward). After heating: Kp = 1.0 < Q = 10 (reverse).
days.early_finishers: Pressure Changes Free Explore with the piston all the way up (Q ≈ 53 > Kp, reverse).

days.title: Student sim work: Ksp and solubility
days.goal: Write Ksp and find molar solubility from Ksp; see what saturation means.
agenda: Warm-up: which is left out of Q: H₂O(l), CO₂(g), CaCO₃(s)?
circulate: Q for a dissolving salt has no denominator.
s = √0.10 = 0.32 M is calculated before the Table tab is opened.
Extra solid is shaken in after equilibrium; Q stays on the K line.
Students say Ksp is a product of concentrations, not "an amount of ions".
days.checkpoint: Molar solubility in pure water: s = 0.32 M; 1875 mg dissolved.
days.early_finishers: Solubility Product Free Explore at 1000 mg and 2500 mg: unsaturated vs. saturated.

days.title: Student sim work: common ion and pH
days.goal: Use the quadratic to find solubility with a common ion; explain why acid dissolves the precipitate.
days.worksheet_pages: pp. 9–10 (Common Ion Effect, pH Effect) + Conclusion
agenda: Warm-up: Le Châtelier for AB(s) ⇌ A⁺ + B⁻ when B⁻ is added
circulate: XB(s) shaken in all the way (4 shakes, [B⁻] = 0.12) before any AB(s).
Q recorded after each of the first 5 H⁺ shakes (the 6th starts the animation).
Graph on p. 10: shape only, no values.
days.checkpoint: With the common ion: s = 0.26 M ([B⁻] = 0.38). After 6 H⁺ shakes the new equilibrium is [A⁺] = 0.40 M, [B⁻] = 0.25 M.
days.early_finishers: Common Ion Free Explore at 250 mg; pH Free Explore with 1000 mg solid and 6 acid additions.

days.title: Grading and wrap-up
agenda: Grading (self-grade with the answer key, or teacher-graded; see the shared grading section)
Discussion: Which changes moved K, and which moved only Q? Link to real salts (CaF₂, Mg(OH)₂)

misconceptions.sim_fix: The sim's own words: at equilibrium both reactions run at the same rate. The concentration lines go flat because the two rates cancel, not because nothing happens.

misconceptions.misconception: At equilibrium the reactant and product concentrations are equal.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Le Chatelier ends at [A] = 0.11, [C] = 0.28; the sim says they "are not equal, just constant."

misconceptions.misconception: Adding product (or changing pressure) changes K.
misconceptions.sim_fix: The K line and the Q = K panel stay at 10 after adding C and D or squeezing the gas; only heating changes Kp (10 → 1.0).

misconceptions.misconception: Adding more solid makes more of it dissolve.
misconceptions.sim_fix: After 1875 mg, extra AB(s) sits on the bottom and Q stays at Ksp = 0.10.

misconceptions.misconception: Ksp is the concentration of the dissolved ions.
misconceptions.sim_fix: Ksp = 0.10, but each ion is 0.32 M: Ksp is the product [A⁺][B⁻].

sim_cautions: Every module starts from its own saved state. The reaction chosen in the first module does not carry into Reaction Quotient, and Pressure/Temperature Changes start from saved numbers, not the students' own.

After raising the temperature, one instruction box says "the forward reaction is being favored." That's wrong: heat is a product here, so the reverse reaction is favored (the next box and the graphs show the reverse).
When the volume is increased, the box still says "the system will consume moles to relieve pressure." With a bigger volume, the system makes more moles of gas.
The flame slider starts in the middle, but the sim treats that as no heat. Tell students to drag it all the way right.
The Q panel can show a 3-digit number for the second product (like 0.214) because it is adjusted to make Q round right. Copy numbers from the Table tab.
The Table tab gives away the equilibrium answer right away; calculate first.
In pH Effect, the Table tab still shows the common-ion numbers, not the pH result; use the Q panel. The red dot on the pH curve slides sideways, which does not mean the solubility stayed the same.
The 1875 mg and 1375 mg in the text don't match the molar solubility ratio; compare molarities, not milligrams.

support: Give a blank ICE-table template with the 'x' rows filled in for p. 2.
Let students use the sim's Table tab to check each ICE row right after they write it.
Provide the quadratic formula on a card for pp. 9–10.
extension: Find Kc for the p. 4 reaction from Kp (needs T; discuss why the sim can't give it).
Find the molar solubility of CaF₂ (Ksp = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹) in water and in 0.10 M NaF.
Predict what squeezing would do to 2A(g) + 3B(g) ⇌ C(g) + 4D(g) (equal gas moles; not one of the sim's gas reactions) and explain why volume would not shift it.

exit_ticket.question: For A + B ⇌ C + D (K = 10), a mix has [A] = [B] = 0.10 M and [C] = [D] = 0.50 M. Which way will it go?
exit_ticket.answer: Q = 0.25/0.010 = 25 > 10, so reverse (toward A and B).

exit_ticket.question: For the exothermic reaction 3A + 4B ⇌ C + 2D, give one change that shifts it to the right without changing Kp.
exit_ticket.answer: Decrease the volume (increase pressure), or add A or B, or remove C or D.

exit_ticket.question: Ksp of AB = 0.10. Is AB more or less soluble in a solution that already has 0.12 M B⁻? Give the molar solubility.
exit_ticket.answer: Less soluble: s = 0.26 M (vs. 0.32 M in pure water).

ap_practice.question: The sim's reaction 3A(g) + 4B(g) ⇌ C(g) + 2D(g) + heat is at equilibrium with Kp = 10 and P_A = 0.74, P_B = 0.36, P_C = 0.25, P_D = 0.51 atm. (a) Show that the system is at equilibrium. (b) The volume is cut to 0.48 of its value at constant T. Calculate Q and predict the shift. (c) Instead, the temperature is raised. State whether Kp increases or decreases, and justify. (d) Explain why adding a catalyst would not change the equilibrium pressures.
ap_practice.answer: (a) Q = 0.25(0.51)²/(0.74³·0.36⁴) = 0.0650/0.00681 ≈ 9.6 ≈ 10 (rounded data), so Q ≈ Kp. (b) Each P × 2.08: Q = 10 × 2.08⁻⁴ = 0.53 < Kp → shifts right (fewer gas moles, 3 vs. 7). (c) Kp decreases: the forward reaction is exothermic, so adding heat favors the reverse (the sim drops Kp from 10 to 1.0). (d) A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally; it does not change Kp or Q, so the system reaches the same equilibrium faster.

ap_practice.question: Multiple choice: A saturated solution of AB(s) ⇌ A⁺(aq) + B⁻(aq) (Ksp = 0.10) has extra solid on the bottom. Which change will dissolve more AB? (A) Add more AB(s). (B) Add XB, a soluble salt with B⁻. (C) Add H⁺, which reacts with B⁻ to form HB. (D) Add more AB(s) and stir.
ap_practice.answer: (C). Removing B⁻ makes Q < Ksp, so more solid dissolves (in the sim, [A⁺] rises from 0.26 to 0.40 M). (A) and (D) do not change Q; (B) adds a common ion and lowers solubility.
